vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: withings-family
Version: 1.1.2

The OpenClaw Withings Family skill is benign. It securely handles OAuth authentication with Withings API, including robust user ID sanitization to prevent path traversal for token files, secure file permissions (0o600) for sensitive tokens, and CSRF protection using a 'state' parameter during the OAuth flow. All network communication is directed to legitimate Withings API endpoints, and there is no evidence of data exfiltration to unauthorized destinations, malicious command execution, persistence mechanisms, or prompt injection attempts in the SKILL.md documentation. The code's functionality is entirely aligned with its stated purpose of fetching health data.

llm.summary: This skill does what it says, but it handles family health records and persistent OAuth tokens with enough storage and consent gaps that users should review it carefully before installing.

dimensions.detail: Network calls to Withings and local file use are proportionate to the purpose, but OAuth access and refresh tokens are written as plaintext JSON with permissions tightened only after creation and chmod failures ignored.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill metadata only requires python3 and Withings client environment variables; there are no package-install hooks, remote payload downloads, startup registration, or tool-wrapping behavior in the artifact.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The instructions disclose OAuth, token refresh, localhost callback use, per-user token files, and scopes, but they do not give a prominent consent/privacy warning for accessing multiple family members' health data or clear token revocation/deletion guidance.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The only persistence found is purpose-aligned credential persistence in ~/.openclaw/withings-family or the legacy ~/.moltbot path, but it stores reusable health-data authorization tokens across sessions without stronger containment or cleanup instructions.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: The Withings health-data purpose matches the bundled Python scripts: they authenticate users, call Withings API endpoints, and print weight, body, activity, and sleep data. The sensitive health-data access is expected but high impact.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Install only if you are comfortable storing Withings OAuth tokens on this machine and using this agent to retrieve sensitive health data. Each family member should explicitly authorize their own account, and users should know where tokens are stored so they can delete them locally and revoke access in Withings if needed. Prefer a trusted single-user machine, and treat the local token directory as sensitive.
llm.findings:
[TP4] expected: Downgraded from a mismatch claim: the SKILL.md body explicitly documents OAuth setup, localhost:18081 callback use, token refresh, and token-file storage, so this is disclosed integration behavior rather than tool poisoning.
[PE3] expected: Overridden as credential theft evidence: the code reads its own per-user Withings token file under the skill-specific directory, not unrelated SSH, AWS, browser, or system credential stores.
[LP3] expected: Partly accepted as a review concern: broad agent tool permissions are not declared in a manifest, but the artifact instructions narrow usage to bundled Python scripts, Withings API endpoints, environment variables, and a skill-specific credential directory.
[SQP-2] expected: Accepted in part: multi-user family health access is central to the skill, but the artifact lacks an explicit consent and privacy warning for each family member whose data may be queried.
[RA2] unexpected: Overridden: I found no cron jobs, startup scripts, background services, or cross-session agent hooks; the referenced setup text is developer-account setup, not unauthorized system persistence.
[SQP-2] expected: Accepted as a material concern: token persistence is expected for OAuth, but both scripts write plaintext token JSON before best-effort chmod and silently continue if permission hardening fails.
[SQP-2] expected: Downgraded to expected behavior: the skill's purpose requires contacting Withings for health data, and the docs identify Withings API use, though a clearer privacy notice would be appropriate.
[T09] unexpected: Accepted as a coding-practice concern: static scan evidence matches the scripts' non-atomic token writes, post-write chmod, and suppressed chmod errors; this is not malicious but weak handling for health OAuth tokens.
